newsitem.title: CHILE: Chilean copper unions grow more restless.
newsitem.headline: Chilean copper unions grow more restless.

text.p: Strikes at two copper mines in northern Chile could signal a newly combative spirit by unions in their efforts to organize workers at large pits, many of them foreign-owned, company and union officials said.

Workers at Broken Hill Proprietary's Escondida mine voted to return to work on Friday after a two-week walkout, but a three-day-old strike at Cominco Ltd's Quebrada Blanca mine continued without a resolution.
A 750-member supervisors' union at state-owned Codelco's Chuquicamata mine has also threatened to strike over a wage dispute but has set no date.

"These labor problems tend to go in cycles but this time there is more conflict than usual. The atmosphere is a little funnier," said an official at a top foreign copper firm, speaking on condition of anonymity.

Although most companies are in a better position to grant wage increases than a few years ago, thanks to generally good copper prices, they are reluctant to lock themselves into generous wage contracts that will cause problems later in a prolonged price slump, he said.
Mining Ministry Benjamin Teplizky said this week the spate of strikes was "a matter of concern" to the government but that it would not intervene directly in private firms' labor relations.

Neither strike will have much effect on Chile's overall copper output -- in the case of Escondida, because only 17 percent of the workforce joined the walkout, and in the case of Quebrada Blanca, because it's a small mine by Chilean standards at 75,000 tonnes a year.

But the Escondida strike was seen as a crucial test of union support because it was the first industrial action in a mainly non-union mine. Only 350 of its 2,000 workers are enrolled in the union, but now any worker will be able to take the union pay package if he chooses.
"This strike is being very closely watched. Its importance goes beyond its importance to Escondida's production levels," said the official, speaking before the strike ended.
The Escondida strike was also accompanied by shrill nationalistic rhetoric of a kind not often heard in Chile these days.

"Escondida is sending all its profits outside the country and we are standing up for the interests of Chile," union president Hugo Fernandez said. "Congratulations to Escondida for now making more copper than Chuquicamata, but this country is selling everything to the foreigners and that's what we're protesting," he told Reuters.

The National Miners' Confederation (CNM), which claims 24,000 affiliates in 90 unions, this week held a congress of private-sector workers in the northern city of Iquique, were it discussed the possiblity of "solidarity strikes" to support individual strikes.

But the CNM has little power or prestige over individual unions and nowhere near the popular draw of miners' confederations in Peru or Bolivia. A similar problem affects Chile's main labor confederation, the CUT, whose May Day march on Thursday was an embarrassing flop that drew only about 2,500 people.
Chile's labor climate has been exacerbated by a government decision to close an unprofitable coal mine, the Lota pit run by state coal company Enacar, putting 1,100 miners out of work.

Apart from Quebrada Blanca, mines where wage contracts expire soon include Mantos Blancos, which said this week it reached a 30- month deal with unions, and Codelco's second largest mine, El Teniente, which comes due at the end of the year.
